title: GOD SAID RETURN THE DONKEY… EVEN IF IT BELONGED TO THE PERSON WHO HURT YOU
paragraphs: GOD SAID RETURN THE DONKEY… EVEN IF IT BELONGED TO THE PERSON WHO HURT YOU

Buried in Exodus 23:4 is a command so uncomfortable that it exposes something many believers would rather keep hidden: God cares not only about how you treat the people you love, but also about what you do when someone who has wronged you suddenly needs your help.
Imagine walking down a dusty road.
The afternoon sun is burning against your skin. You're tired. You've been carrying burdens nobody knows about. And somewhere along that road, you notice a donkey wandering alone.
No owner. No rope in anyone's hand. Just a lost animal, vulnerable and separated from the person who depends on it.
You move closer.
Then you recognize it.
You know exactly whose donkey this is.
And suddenly, everything changes.
Because this animal belongs to someone who has made your life miserable.
Someone who humiliated you.
Someone who spoke against you when you weren't there to defend yourself.
Someone who may have celebrated when things went wrong in your life.
And now, standing right in front of you, is something that belongs to that very person.
Nobody is watching.
Nobody knows you've found it.
You could turn around and keep walking.
You could tell yourself that it's none of your business.
You could even convince yourself that perhaps God is finally allowing that person to experience a little of the trouble they've caused you.
After all, wouldn't that feel like justice?
But then Scripture interrupts your thoughts.
"If thou meet thine enemy's ox or his ass going astray, thou shalt surely bring it back to him again." — Exodus 23:4, KJV
Read that again.
Not your friend's donkey.
Not your brother's donkey.
Not the donkey belonging to someone who has treated you with kindness.
Your enemy's donkey.
And God says to bring it back.
There is something almost scandalous about that command.
Because the Lord did not ask whether the enemy deserved the animal's return.
He did not ask whether the enemy had apologized.
He did not ask whether the enemy had finally admitted what he did.
God simply commanded His people to do what was right.
Even when doing right would benefit someone who had done them wrong.
And perhaps the most uncomfortable part of this ancient command is that it was never really just about a donkey.
It was about the human heart.
The same heart that can worship God with lifted hands on Sunday and quietly enjoy another person's suffering on Monday.
The same heart that can pray for forgiveness while secretly hoping someone else never receives mercy.
The same heart that says, "Lord, bless me," but struggles to say, "Lord, have mercy on the person who hurt me."
And before we rush to explain why our situation is different, we need to hear what God actually said.
Because the Hebrew makes the command even more striking.
In the original text of Exodus 23:4, we read:
כִּי תִפְגַּע שׁוֹר אֹיִבְךָ אוֹ חֲמֹרוֹ תֹּעֶה הָשֵׁב תְּשִׁיבֶנּוּ לוֹ
Ki tifga shor oyivkha o chamoro to'eh, hashev teshivennu lo.
A close English rendering is:
"If you encounter your enemy's ox or his donkey wandering away, you shall certainly return it to him."
Notice the expression הָשֵׁב תְּשִׁיבֶנּוּ — hashev teshivennu.
The Hebrew uses an infinitive absolute alongside a finite verb from the same verbal root, a construction that intensifies the command.
The meaning is not merely, "It might be nice if you returned it."
It carries the force of "You must indeed return it."
There is no room in the command for pretending that hatred makes dishonesty acceptable.
And that matters because, in the ancient world, an ox or donkey was not merely a possession someone could casually replace.
These animals were important to agricultural work, transportation, and the movement of goods. Losing one could create a serious practical and financial burden.
God was commanding His people to protect even an enemy from a preventable loss.
Think about that.
The person might have been hostile.
The relationship might have been broken.
The resentment might have been real.
But the animal still needed to be returned.
God did not allow personal hostility to cancel the obligation to act justly.
And the next verse goes further.
"If thou see the ass of him that hateth thee lying under his burden, and wouldest forbear to help him, thou shalt surely help with him." — Exodus 23:5, KJV
Here the situation becomes even more personal.
You are no longer simply finding a wandering animal.
You are witnessing the donkey of someone who hates you struggling beneath a burden.
And the law directs you to help.

The Hebrew wording of Exodus 23:5 is difficult in places, and English translations differ in how they express its details. But its central instruction is clear: hostility toward the owner must not become an excuse for withholding necessary assistance.
Imagine the scene.
The donkey is down.
The load is heavy.
Its owner is struggling.
You recognize the man.
And somewhere inside you, a voice whispers:
"Remember what he did to you."
"Remember what he said about your family."
"Remember the nights you couldn't sleep because of him."
"Why should you help?"
And then another truth confronts you.
Because the God who sees your suffering also sees what you choose to do with it.
He sees the difference between seeking justice and enjoying revenge.
He sees when a wounded heart begins turning its pain into permission to wound others.
And He sees the moment when obedience costs you something.
This is where the command becomes painfully relevant.
Because most of us will never encounter an enemy's lost donkey.
But we will encounter an enemy's vulnerability.
Perhaps the person who betrayed you is now struggling financially.
Perhaps the relative who humiliated you is facing a crisis.
Perhaps the coworker who damaged your reputation now needs information only you can provide.
Perhaps the person who mocked your faith is suddenly asking you to pray.
And suddenly, the question is no longer about an animal on an ancient road.
It is about whether you will let another person's wrongdoing determine your own character.
You may never have stolen anything from that person.
You may never have openly sought revenge.
But have you ever quietly enjoyed hearing that someone who hurt you was suffering?
Have you ever withheld a kindness you knew was right because you wanted them to feel what you felt?
Have you ever called bitterness "discernment" because the word sounded more spiritual?
Have you ever said, "God will deal with them," while secretly hoping His dealing would look exactly like your revenge?
That is where this passage reaches beneath our religious vocabulary.
Because God is not merely interested in whether our hands appear innocent.
He also cares about what our hearts are becoming.
And this is why Exodus 23:4 belongs to something much larger than a collection of ancient agricultural regulations.
The command appears within the covenant laws given to Israel after the exodus from Egypt.
The Lord had rescued His people from oppression and was teaching them how to live as a community under His authority.
The surrounding instructions address truthfulness, justice, false testimony, partiality, and the treatment of vulnerable people.
In other words, God was forming a people whose conduct would reflect His righteous character.
They were not permitted to manipulate justice for their friends.
And they were not permitted to abandon justice when dealing with their enemies.
That is an extraordinary standard.
Because human beings often find it easy to recognize wrongdoing when it is committed against someone they love.
But when the victim is someone they dislike, their moral certainty can become strangely flexible.
God's law confronts that double standard.
Right does not become wrong because it benefits your enemy. And wrong does not become right because your enemy suffers from it.
There is another important truth here.
The law did not require the injured person to pretend that the enemy was trustworthy.
It did not command the victim to deny the existence of hostility.
In fact, the text explicitly identifies the other person as an enemy.
God acknowledged the broken relationship while still requiring righteous conduct.
That distinction matters.
Especially for someone reading this who has experienced betrayal, abuse, manipulation, or serious injustice.
Returning a lost animal is not the same as restoring unrestricted access to your life.
Helping someone in genuine need does not require remaining in an unsafe relationship.
Forgiveness does not mean denying wrongdoing.
And showing mercy does not mean abandoning appropriate boundaries, accountability, or the pursuit of justice.
The Lord never needed evil to be called good in order to command His people to do good.
He was teaching something far more powerful.
You can refuse to become cruel without pretending that cruelty never happened to you.
And then, centuries later, Jesus Christ stood before people who knew the Scriptures and revealed just how far the love of God reaches.
"But I say unto you, Love your enemies, bless them that curse you, do good to them that hate you, and pray for them which despitefully use you, and persecute you." — Matthew 5:44, KJV
Jesus was not contradicting the righteous concern already present in Exodus.
He was bringing the moral demand into unmistakable focus.
The God who commanded Israel to return an enemy's donkey was now calling His hearers to love their enemies.
Not merely to avoid harming them.
Not merely to tolerate them from a distance.
But to seek their good in ways consistent with truth and righteousness.
The Greek of Matthew 5:44 begins with these words:
ἐγὼ δὲ λέγω ὑμῖν, ἀγαπᾶτε τοὺς ἐχθροὺς ὑμῶν
Egō de legō hymin, agapate tous echthrous hymōn.
"But I say to you, love your enemies."
The verb ἀγαπᾶτε — agapate is an imperative: a command to love.
It does not require manufacturing warm feelings toward someone who has hurt you.
It calls for a love expressed through a commitment to what is good and right.
That love can include prayer, mercy, truthful confrontation, and necessary boundaries.
And in Matthew 5:45, Jesus points to the Father's generosity, explaining that God makes His sun rise on the evil and the good and sends rain on the just and the unjust.
Consider the picture.
The same sunlight reaches the home of the person who has blessed you and the home of the person who has cursed you.
The same rain falls on the field of the grateful and the field of the ungrateful.
God's ordinary kindness is not restricted to people who have earned it.
And Jesus calls His disciples to reflect the Father's character.
But now we come to the part of the story that changes everything.
Because there is something far more astonishing than a man returning his enemy's donkey.
There is a Savior who gave His life for His enemies.
And if we miss that, we have missed the deepest Christian significance of this passage.
Listen to the apostle Paul.
"For if, when we were enemies, we were reconciled to God by the death of his Son, much more, being reconciled, we shall be saved by his life." — Romans 5:10, KJV
When we were enemies.
Not when we had finally cleaned ourselves up.
Not when we had accumulated enough good deeds.
Not when we had become worthy of His attention.
When we were enemies.
The Greek word Paul uses is ἐχθροὶ — echthroi, meaning "enemies."
The same basic Greek word family appears in Jesus' command to love our enemies.
And here is the breathtaking reality of the Gospel.
Jesus did not merely tell us to love our enemies. He loved us when we were His enemies.
Romans 5:8 declares:
"But God commendeth his love toward us, in that, while we were yet sinners, Christ died for us."
While we were yet sinners.
Before our repentance could ever become a reason for boasting.
Before we could offer God a record of obedience that would make us deserving.
Christ died for us.
And suddenly, the lost donkey on the dusty road becomes a doorway into a far greater truth.
Not because Exodus 23:4 secretly predicts the crucifixion or because the donkey is a coded symbol of Jesus.
Scripture does not say that.
But because the command reveals a pattern of righteousness that finds its fullest expression in the character and saving work of Christ.
God commands His people to act mercifully toward enemies.
And in the Gospel, we behold the Son of God extending saving grace to sinners who could never earn it.
Think of Calvary.
Jesus is hanging on the cross.
His body has been wounded.
He has been mocked.
His garments have been divided.
He is suffering beneath the weight of a punishment He did not deserve.
And Luke records these words:
"Father, forgive them; for they know not what they do." — Luke 23:34, KJV
Those words do not mean that every person present was automatically forgiven without repentance or faith.
They reveal the extraordinary mercy of Christ toward those participating in His suffering.
He was not excusing their evil.
He was praying in the midst of it.
And the One who prayed for His persecutors was accomplishing the redemption through which forgiveness would be offered to sinners.
What kind of love is this?
What kind of King wears a crown of thorns?
What kind of Savior prays while His enemies mock Him?
What kind of mercy does not wait for its recipients to become lovable?
The kind that comes from Jesus Christ.
And perhaps this is why the command in Exodus is so difficult for us.
Because it exposes how naturally we want mercy for ourselves and consequences for everyone else.
We want God to remember our tears.
But we sometimes want Him to ignore the tears of those who hurt us.
We want grace to cover our worst moments.
But we struggle when grace reaches people whose worst moments wounded us.
We want the Father to be patient with our unfinished transformation.
But we can become impatient when another sinner has not changed quickly enough.
And the cross stands before all of us, dismantling our pride.
Not by declaring sin insignificant.
But by showing how serious sin truly is and how astonishing God's grace truly is.
Jesus did not die because evil was harmless.
He died because sin required redemption, and we could not save ourselves.
And the risen Christ now calls us to repent, believe the Gospel, and follow Him.
That means the Christian response to an enemy is not built on pretending we have never been hurt.
It is built on remembering that we ourselves live by undeserved mercy.
Maybe you are reading this while carrying a wound nobody else understands.
Maybe there is a name you cannot hear without feeling your chest tighten.
Maybe the betrayal was not a small misunderstanding.
Maybe it cost you years.
Maybe you lost friendships, opportunities, peace, or a sense of safety.
And every time someone tells you to forgive, it feels as though they are asking you to say the pain never mattered.
But the Gospel does not ask you to call your suffering imaginary.
Jesus knows what betrayal feels like.
He knows what abandonment feels like.
He knows what it is to be falsely accused.
And He knows what it is to suffer unjustly.
Your wounds matter to Him.
But so does what those wounds are doing inside you.
Because bitterness can become a burden you carry long after the person who hurt you has stopped thinking about what happened.
And sometimes the most difficult act of obedience is not confronting the person who wounded you.
Sometimes it is surrendering your private desire to see them destroyed.
Sometimes it is praying, through tears, "Lord, I don't know how to love this person rightly. But I don't want hatred to become the ruler of my heart."
That prayer may not instantly remove the pain.
Forgiveness can be a costly process.
Trust may need to be rebuilt through genuine repentance and changed behavior.
Some relationships may never be safe to restore.
But obedience can begin with a heart that is willing to place vengeance into God's hands.
Romans 12:19 says:
"Dearly beloved, avenge not yourselves, but rather give place unto wrath: for it is written, Vengeance is mine; I will repay, saith the Lord."
And just a few verses later:
"Be not overcome of evil, but overcome evil with good." — Romans 12:21, KJV
There it is again.
The same moral direction we encountered on that dusty road in Exodus.
Do not let another person's evil become the blueprint for your own behavior.
Do not repay cruelty with cruelty.
Do not surrender your conscience to resentment.
Overcome evil with good.
Not because evil is harmless.
Not because justice no longer matters.
But because God remains righteous, and His people are called to reflect His character.
There may be someone you need to stop speaking about with contempt.
Someone whose hardship you need to stop celebrating.
Someone you need to pray for, even if you must do so from a safe distance.
There may be a wrong you need to confess because you have used someone else's sin to justify your own.
Or perhaps you are the person who has become someone else's enemy.
Perhaps you are the one who betrayed trust.
The one who spread the rumor.
The one who walked away without taking responsibility.
The one who keeps saying, "That's just how I am," because genuine repentance would require painful change.
Then this passage is speaking to you too.
Because the Gospel is not merely an invitation for wounded people to release revenge.
It is also an invitation for guilty people to stop hiding, turn from sin, and seek the mercy of Christ.
You cannot undo every consequence of your past.
You cannot demand that someone trust you again.
But by God's grace, you can repent.
You can confess.
You can make restitution where appropriate.
You can begin walking in truth.
And you can discover that your worst chapter does not have to become your final chapter.
This is why we keep returning to the message:
Not because Jesus erases history.
Not because He makes the consequences of sin disappear on demand.
But because through His death and resurrection, He offers forgiveness, reconciliation with God, and a transformed life to all who turn to Him in faith.
Second Corinthians 5:17 declares:
"Therefore if any man be in Christ, he is a new creature: old things are passed away; behold, all things are become new."
The scandal is real.
The sin is real.
The damage may be real.
But the grace of God in Jesus Christ is real too.
And His grace does more than make us feel better about our past.
It teaches us to live differently.
It teaches us to tell the truth when lying would be easier.
To practice justice when favoritism would be more comfortable.
To show mercy when resentment offers a more satisfying story.
To return what belongs to another person even when that person has wronged us.
And to remember that our obedience is not the price we pay to purchase God's love.
It is the fruit of a life being changed by His love.
Maybe that is the question you need to carry with you today.
Not, "Does my enemy deserve kindness?"
But, "What would faithfulness to Jesus require of me in this moment?"
You may not be able to fix the relationship.
You may not receive an apology.
You may not see the person change.
But you can ask God for the strength to remain faithful.
And when you fail, you can return to the Savior who forgives repentant sinners and continues His transforming work in His people.
You can simply write "Jesus, change my heart."

And if Christ has helped you forgive someone you once believed you could never forgive, consider sharing a little of your testimony. Your story may give another wounded believer courage to seek God's help.
You do not need to reveal private details or name the person who hurt you. The Lord knows the story.
And someone reading your words may realize they are not alone in their struggle.
Maybe it is a friend who has been consumed by resentment.
Maybe it is a family member trapped in an old conflict.
Maybe it is someone who believes Christianity is only about religious appearances and has never encountered the life-changing grace of Jesus.
Save it too.

Because the next time someone hurts you, the next time resentment rises, or the next time you are tempted to celebrate another person's downfall, you may need to return to the quiet, uncomfortable command of Exodus 23:4.
There are people around us who are spiritually hungry but do not know where to begin.
People who own a Bible but feel intimidated when they open it.
People who have spent years around Christianity without understanding the Gospel.
People who are ashamed of their past and wonder whether Jesus would still receive them.
We want to keep reaching them with Scripture-centered teaching, honest conversations about repentance, encouragement for the weary, and the life-giving message of salvation through Jesus Christ.
Second Corinthians 9:7 says:
"Every man according as he purposeth in his heart, so let him give; not grudgingly, or of necessity: for God loveth a cheerful giver."
That is the spirit of this invitation.
Not pressure.
Not guilt.
But a genuine opportunity to participate in work you believe is worth supporting.
These products are not the heart of the mission.
Christ is.
We want Scripture to be studied.
We want the Gospel to be understood.
We want wounded people to find hope in Christ.
We want struggling believers to become grounded in truth.
And we want those who have wandered far from God to know that the invitation to repent and believe in Jesus Christ still stands.
Whatever you decide, do not miss the greater invitation in this passage.
God is calling His people to a kind of righteousness that reaches into the places where our resentment hides.
And Jesus Christ offers the grace we need to repent, believe, and begin living that righteousness from a changed heart.
One day, you may find yourself standing at your own version of that dusty road.
You may see an opportunity to do good for someone who has done you wrong.
Nobody may be watching.
Nobody may thank you.
Nobody may ever know what obedience cost you.
But the Lord will know.
And in that moment, you may remember a wandering donkey, an ancient command, and a crucified Savior who loved His enemies.
You may remember that mercy is not weakness.
That forgiveness is not the denial of justice.
That grace is not permission to continue sinning.
And that the love of Jesus is powerful enough to transform a heart that once wanted revenge.
The donkey was never the greatest burden on that road.
The heaviest thing you may need to lay down is the hatred you've been carrying toward the person who hurt you.
